items.title: Babies have a special fat that wastes energy as heat — on purpose
items.claim: Brown adipose tissue, found in newborns and hibernating mammals, contains mitochondria packed with a protein (UCP1) that lets protons leak back across the inner membrane WITHOUT making ATP. The energy is dissipated as pure heat.
items.prompt: Why deliberately uncouple respiration from ATP synthesis?

options.text: It's a mistake the body cannot fix
Newborns and small mammals lose heat fast (high surface area to volume ratio). Brown fat lets them generate large amounts of heat on demand without shivering — burning fat directly to warmth

items.reveal:
In ordinary mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps protons OUT; ATP synthase lets them back IN, capturing the energy as ATP.

In brown adipose tissue, the protein UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1, also called thermogenin) provides an alternative route for protons to flow back in — bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient still forms; the energy still flows; but it dissipates as heat rather than ATP.

Brown fat is brown because it's packed with mitochondria (iron-rich cytochromes). It's especially abundant in newborn humans (around the neck and shoulder blades) and in hibernating mammals (which use it to wake from torpor).

Adults retain some brown fat, more in lean people; PET-CT scans light it up. There's active research into pharmacologically activating brown fat as an anti-obesity strategy.

The drug DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) chemically uncouples mitochondria. It does cause weight loss — but also fatal hyperthermia. It's been banned for human use for nearly a century, though it still kills bodybuilders occasionally.
items.why: Inefficiency seems like a flaw. The body uses controlled mitochondrial inefficiency as a thermostat — and biotech is trying to weaponise it against obesity.

items.title: Your brain is rinsed clean of waste only when you sleep
items.claim: The brain has no lymphatic vessels for waste removal. Instead, during sleep, cerebrospinal fluid flows through brain tissue via the glymphatic system, washing out metabolic waste including amyloid-beta (linked to Alzheimer's). The pathway is 60% more open during sleep than waking.
items.prompt: What changes between sleep and wake?

options.text: During sleep, brain interstitial space expands (~60%), allowing CSF to flow rapidly through it; during waking, the space is smaller and flow is reduced. Cellular debris and protein aggregates clear faster while you sleep
Waste is excreted through the eyes

items.reveal:
Maiken Nedergaard's lab (Xie et al., Science 2013) discovered that the brain's waste-clearance pathway is dramatically more active during sleep.

Mechanism: cerebrospinal fluid enters the brain along arterial perivascular spaces, mixes with interstitial fluid, and exits along venous perivascular spaces, carrying waste with it. Aquaporin-4 channels on astrocyte endfeet are critical.

During sleep, brain cells shrink (~60% increase in interstitial volume), allowing much faster bulk flow. The amount of amyloid-beta (a protein implicated in Alzheimer's) cleared during sleep is roughly double that of waking.

Mice with disrupted glymphatic flow accumulate amyloid-beta and develop cognitive decline. Chronic poor sleep is increasingly linked epidemiologically to Alzheimer's risk in humans.

This is one of the strongest known reasons for sleep — and was discovered only in 2013. Sleep had been one of biology's biggest unsolved 'why' questions.

Other sleep functions: memory consolidation (especially REM), synaptic homeostasis (downscaling synapse strength to make room for new learning), immune function. The brain seems to use sleep for many heavy housekeeping operations.
items.why: Sleep was a mystery for decades. One major answer turns out to be: the brain literally rinses itself. Skipping sleep means accumulating molecular debris.

items.title: Your body can make antibodies against molecules that don't exist yet
items.claim: Humans have about 20,000 genes. We make perhaps 10 to the 11 different antibody molecules — far more than our genome could encode directly. Including antibodies against viruses we'll never meet.
items.prompt: How do we generate such enormous antibody diversity?

options.text: Each antibody is encoded by a separate gene

V(D)J recombination — during B cell development, gene segments (V, D, J) are randomly chosen and joined with imprecise cuts, and then somatic hypermutation refines the result during an immune response
Antibodies are made up new for each encounter from scratch
The genome reshuffles itself constantly in all cells

items.reveal_title: Tonegawa's discovery — recombination in somatic cells
items.reveal:
Susumu Tonegawa (Nobel 1987) showed that B cells deliberately rearrange their immunoglobulin genes. Each B cell randomly picks one V, one D and one J segment for the heavy chain (V and J for the light chain), joins them with imprecise junctions (adding/deleting nucleotides), and pairs heavy with light. The combinatorial maths gives about 10 to the 11 possible specificities from a few hundred gene segments.

Once a B cell encounters its antigen, somatic hypermutation introduces additional point mutations into the variable region, and selection retains the best binders (affinity maturation).

The result is an immune system that can respond to virtually any molecular shape — including ones never seen before, like artificial drugs.
items.why: Genome size limits direct encoding. The immune system uses combinatorics and somatic mutation to overshoot what the genome alone could specify.
